newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Rival Serb leaders due to meet to defuse stand-off.
newsitem.headline: Rival Serb leaders due to meet to defuse stand-off.

text.p: Feuding Bosnian Serb leaders plan to hold crisis talks on Sunday to defuse an increasingly tense stand-off between President Biljana Plavsic and hardliners loyal to former Serb leader and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.

Plavsic was expected to meet her rival Momcilo Krajisnik, Serb member of the Bosnian presidency, after a week-long confrontation which has raised fears that the country's peace process could be derailed.
Krajisnik, a key ally of Karadzic, told reporters he would meet Plavsic in the eastern town of Bijeljina, after he came under intense pressure from U.S. special envoy Robert Gelbard.
Gelbard and other Western envoys have warned the hardliners grouped around Karadzic that they must abide by a presidential decision to dissolve the Bosnian Serb parliament.
The U.S. envoy to the Balkans said Plavsic had acted legally and said the conflict would be addressed at a NATO summit in Madrid on Sunday.
Thousands of people demonstrated in support of Plavsic in the northwest town of Banja Luka for the second day running as hardliners held an assembly session in defiance of the president's decision.
The hardliners in Karadzic's party failed to secure a two-thirds majority needed to launch a recall vote against Plavsic and ended up amending laws to suit their purposes.
The new law allowed a majority of deputies present to vote for Plavsic's removal in a referendum.
"What kind of an assembly do you have if you change the law when you don't have a majority?" Carlos Westendorp, the international High Representative to Bosnia, told Reuters.
As far as the international community was concerned, "there is no assembly," Westendorp said. The hardliners' moves on Saturday were a "a sign that they are not at ease".
The ruling Serb Democratic Party (SDS) also tried to strip Plavsic of authority as commander-in-chief by radically altering a defence council advising the president.

If the crisis continued, mediators were concerned that two rival governments would emerge in the western and eastern halves of Serb territory, one in Banja Luka, and one directed by Karadzic in Pale, outside Sarajevo.
No shots have been fired so far in the power struggle but the NATO-led peace force has stepped up its presence in Serb territory to ensure no violence breaks out.
The feud between Plavsic and Karadzic's circle erupted a week ago when she demanded the suspension of the powerful interior minister, Dragan Kijac, a long-time Karadzic loyalist.
Plavsic delivered scathing attacks against Karadzic and his police, accusing them of running "shameful" smuggling deals at the expense of ordinary Serbs living in abject poverty.
Although hardliners were trying to isolate Plavsic by relying on the police and official media, her allegations struck a chord among many Serbs, especially in Banja Luka.
Plavsic was a loyal deputy to Karadzic during the 1992-95 Bosnian war and supported his "ethnic cleansing" campaign against Moslems and Croats.
After she was elected president of Bosnia's Serb entity, she has refused to play the obedient role devised by Pale.
Although she remains a nationalist ideologue, Western envoys say she has been willing to obey the Dayton accords to win reconstruction aid and end the Serbs' diplomatic isolation.
Karadzic, twice indicted by a U.N. war crimes tribunal, reluctantly stepped down as president last year under heavy international pressure.

His blatant intervention against Plavsic had reinforced a growing realisation that no lasting peace could be established as long as Karadzic and other war crimes suspects were allowed to remain free, some diplomats said.
The outgoing deputy to the High Representative, Michael Steiner, indicated that Western countries considering arresting Karadzic to face charges before the U.N. war crimes tribunal.
"Especially after recent developments, (Western) capitals are aware that it is an unavoidable task if one really wants the Dayton agreement implemented," Steiner said.
